paper_title: $Δτ$-Bench: Pushing Agents Toward a Moving Capability

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce $Δτ$-Bench, an executable agent benchmark that models the structural evolution of large tool ecosystems. In $Δτ$-Bench, independently evolving services continually reshape how tasks can be accomplished: familiar tools may disappear or be replaced, while more efficient alternatives emerge amid overlapping functionality and noisy documentation. Against this moving capability frontier, we evaluate whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly revise their accumulated procedural knowledge, bringing together demands that existing benchmarks fail to examine. $Δτ$-Bench comprises 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks across 42 domains and six successive ecosystem states generated through capability-preserving transformations. Our evaluation shows that even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieves only 42.3% task success, while initial gains from existing skill-learning methods can not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves. These findings motivate Steward, an ecosystem manager that jointly manages tools and procedural knowledge through incremental skill maintenance and dynamic provisioning during task execution. Experiments show that Steward sustains higher task success across ecosystem changes with lower skill-maintenance overhead, while improving both recovery from disrupted workflows and adoption of more efficient alternatives.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are reshaping how users interact with software, enabling them to delegate goals through natural language and have actions carried out on their behalf (Qin et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2023; Xi et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2024). Through tool interfaces, agents can access external services and coordinate multi-step operations to fulfill these goals (Qin et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025; Qiao et al., 2024b; Dong et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2025a). This opens the prospect of unified service interface: users specify what they need, while agents take responsibility for finding and orchestrating the capabilities required to deliver it. As shown in Fig. 1, imagine large company deploying an agent as unified entry point to its services. Behind this single interface lies large tool ecosystem, with individual departments independently maintaining and updating their own tools. Overlapping functionality and noisy or inaccurate descriptions make this catalog difficult to navigate, while ongoing updates continually reshape the available paths through it. As departments retire or replace tools, established workflows may break, forcing the agent to search the broader ecosystem for alternatives. Meanwhile, newly added tools may enable more Equal Contribution. Corresponding Author. 1Code: zjunlp/delta-tau-bench, Dataset: Figure 1: Agent adaptation in evolving tool ecosystems. Tool updates can invalidate learned workflows or introduce better alternatives, while overlapping tools and noisy descriptions hinder discovery. zjunlp/delta-tau-bench Preprint. efficient workflows, but these opportunities can remain hidden among the many services while familiar procedures continue to succeed. Keeping pace therefore requires the agent to actively discover how the companys changing capabilities can be used and revise its procedural knowledge accordingly. Otherwise, successful task execution can conceal growing gap between what the ecosystem offers and what the agent has learned to accomplish with it. Evaluating this challenge requires comparing an agents behavior with what the current ecosystem makes possible for the same task. Existing benchmarks assess large-scale tool retrieval and stateful execution (Shi et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025a; Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), cost-aware replanning under changing execution conditions (Liu et al., 2026e; Valmeekam et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Kokel et al., 2025), and robustness to tool evolution (Liu et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2025b). However, these settings largely examine these abilities separately, generally keeping service structures fixed or constraining tool discovery when services change. They leave open whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly update their procedural knowledge as large ecosystem evolves. Addressing this question calls for an evaluation of sustained agent competence against the moving capability frontier of an evolving tool ecosystem. To address this gap, we introduce τ -Bench, an executable benchmark spanning the full tool-use lifecycle in large, evolving ecosystems. It comprises stateful services across 42 domains and 1,588 validated tasks requiring multi-turn user interaction. Starting from these services, we generate six successive ecosystem states through capability-preserving transformations that refine, split, or integrate tool interfaces. Older and newer tools may coexist or replace one another, changing how tasks can be completed while preserving access to the underlying capabilities. For each state, we identify the most efficient task paths within the constructed solution space and use them as references for evaluating agent behavior. By assessing tool discovery alongside stateful execution against these evolving references, τ -Bench measures whether agents recover from disrupted workflows and exploit efficiency gains that successful execution alone may fail to reveal. Evaluation shows that current agents struggle to sustain reliable and efficient execution in evolving tool ecosystems, with even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieving only 42.3% task success. Existing skill-learning methods provide initial gains, but these do not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves, and skill maintenance can also incur substantial overhead. These findings highlight the need to manage accumulated knowledge together with the changing tools through which it is applied. We therefore introduce STEWARD, an ecosystem manager that coordinates the full lifecycle of tools and skills as coupled resource system, from knowledge updates to downstream use. By tracking skilltool dependencies, STEWARD incrementally maintains the skill library as tools change, preserving reusable experience. During execution, it jointly supplies relevant tools and procedural guidance, adapting this resource selection as the task unfolds. This connects what the agent learns and retains with what it can effectively use in the current ecosystem. Experiments show that STEWARD sustains stronger performance across ecosystem changes while reducing skill-maintenance overhead. Its benefits extend beyond keeping existing workflows functional to exploiting more efficient solutions as they become available. Further analyses show that preserving and selectively updating accumulated knowledge is more effective than repeatedly rebuilding it, while jointly providing tools and skills yields benefits that neither resource provides alone.

sections.title: 3.1 EXECUTABLE ENVIRONMENT AND TASK CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Domain-Grounded Stateful Environments. Following Sun et al. (2026), we expand seed domains into specialized, role-specific scenarios grouped by related activities. For each group, we construct entity schemas and an entityrelationship graph around primary user role. These define coherent service blueprints specifying users, maintained information, and functions. Validated functions are deterministically converted into interfaces with natural-language descriptions and JSON Schemas, forming the tool-call action space Atool. We instantiate entity records and relationships in mock database, validating schema and relational constraints to obtain the initial external state sE 0 . MCP services implement these interfaces under policies governing parameter semantics, invocation constraints, state changes, and dependencies, returning results or errors in declared formats. Grounded Task Synthesis and Execution Validation. From the interfaces and policies, we derive tool-dependency graph and sample paths under dependency and parameter-flow constraints. Sampling favors state-querying starts while allowing state-changing starts when their preconditions hold. To increase task difficulty, we join paths sharing function and repeat intermediate subpaths, retaining only sequences with coherent function ordering, parameter flow, and task objectives. Conditioned on the service blueprints, interfaces, policies, and database summaries, we generate natural-language task templates and user intents requiring every sampled function for single coherent objective. An independent evaluator screens templates for motivation clarity, coherence, function coverage, naturalness, and specificity. For retained templates, we ground arguments in user-known information or preceding tool outputs and replay instantiated sequences from sE 0 against the MCP service. Only instances where every action succeeds with the intended observations and state transitions are retained, yielding reference trajectories τgold and terminal external states sE gold. Task-Conditioned User Simulation. An independent LLM-based user agent follows general protocol and private handbook specifying the complete intent u, motivation, grounded user informa3 Preprint. tion, and disclosure rules. We generate an initial request o0 that expresses the users immediate need while leaving some task details for subsequent dialogue. When the evaluated agent asks for missing task information, the user agent provides the corresponding details from the handbook in accordance with the task-specific disclosure rules. Throughout the dialogue, the user agent speaks from the users perspective, progressively disclosing only grounded information without mentioning functions or execution plans. Responses are conditioned on the protocol, handbook, and visible dialogue, which contains only natural-language messages exchanged between the agents. Interaction ends when the user agent indicates that its intent is satisfied or the request is outside the service scope.

sections.title: 4 EVALUATING AGENTS IN EVOLVING TOOL ECOSYSTEMS
sections.content: Evaluation Setup. We evaluate whether current powerful models can reach the capability frontier of each of six tool-ecosystem versions and whether automated skill methods can track this frontier by accumulating experiences as the ecosystem evolves. For models that expose configurable reasoning effort, we set it to high and retain the recommended defaults for all other inference parameters. The user model is fixed to DeepSeek-V3.2 throughout all experiments. All controlled model ablations and all comparisons in the skill-method study use DeepSeek-V3.2 as the task model.

sections.title: 4.1 MODELS STRUGGLE TO REACH THE CURRENT FRONTIER
sections.content: We examine whether current models can independently reach the capability frontier of each toolecosystem version. As shown in Tab. 1, even the strongest model (Gemini-3.6-Flash) and harness (Codex-GPT-5.5) achieve SRs of only 41.65% and 42.27%, respectively, while neither exceeds 30% in Stepor Cost-SPE. Tool retrieval exhibits pronounced imbalance: Codex-GPT-5.5 retrieves 90.36% of the relevant tools, yet attains only 19.90% precision and an F1 score of 32.04%, pattern that persists across models, indicating that models often include relevant tools but struggle to exclude irrelevant candidates from the broader ecosystem. Moreover, success does not necessarily imply efficient execution. For example, although DeepSeek-V4-Pro slightly outperforms GLM-5.2 in SR, it trails in both Stepand Cost-SPE, and Stepand Cost-SPE/SR. We next conduct controlled diagnostic to probe barriers to identifying and executing efficient tool-use paths. Specifically, we compare Standard with four increasingly informative conditions. Domain Tools restricts retrieval to the task domain, whereas Task Tools provides all tools used by the task across versions to test whether models can distinguish currently available and efficient options from unavailable or overlapping alternatives. Oracle Tools retains only relevant, current-version tools, while Oracle Path additionally provides the reference tool path to isolate path-planning difficulty. As shown in Fig. 3, SR and both SPE variants rise steadily from Standard through Domain Tools and Task Tools to Oracle Tools, whereas Oracle Path yields no further improvement. The gains from Standard to Domain Tools and Task Tools show that removing domainand task-irrelevant candidates eases tool identification. More importantly, the pronounced SPE/SR gain from Task Tools to Oracle Tools shows that models struggle to distinguish efficient, version-valid options from unavailable or overlapping alternatives. The negligible change under Oracle Path instead indicates that the remaining gap lies less in high-level planning than in correctly and efficiently using available tools. Overall, current models struggle both to retrieve relevant tools precisely and to execute their efficient realizations in evolving ecosystems. Figure 3: Ablations on Tool Provision.

sections.title: 4.2 SKILL METHODS STRUGGLE TO TRACK THE MOVING FRONTIER
sections.content: Our preceding diagnosis shows that models struggle primarily to identify and efficiently execute currently valid tool-use paths in an evolving ecosystem. So, we examine whether automated skill generation and optimization methods can overcome this limitation by accumulating experience. As shown in Fig. 4, we compare four automated skill methods: EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026), AutoSkill 6 Preprint. Figure 5: Overview of STEWARD. As an ecosystem manager, STEWARD maintains shared tool and skill resources, updating hierarchical skills using verified experience and current tool availability. It initializes the task agents view through planning and retrieval, then dynamically updates it as capability gaps emerge. (Yang et al., 2026b), Trace2Skill (Ni et al., 2026), SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026a), against the No Skill baseline across six ecosystem versions (Please refer to Appx. for baseline details). At v1, all four methods outperform No Skill in SR and both SPE variants, showing that accumulated experience provides useful initial guidance. However, these gains do not persist uniformly: AutoSkill falls below No Skill in SR at v3 and v5, while AutoSkill and EvoSkill also underperform it in SPE at several intermediate versions. This limitation is more pronounced in DAR: at v3, both EvoSkill and AutoSkill drop to 0 in Stepand Cost-DAR, whereas No Skill retains 11.11% and 10.25%, respectively. Moreover, No Skill achieves the highest Cost-IDR at v2 and both DAR variants at v5, indicating that accumulated skills do not consistently improve adaptation to ecosystem changes. Accordingly, although SkillOpt leads in SR and SPE across versions, its advantage does not extend consistently to IDR and DAR, showing that stronger current-version performance does not necessarily imply better frontier tracking. This stronger current-version performance also incurs substantially higher maintenance costs, with SkillOpt averaging about 3,000 K/task for skill generation and optimization, roughly two to three times the other methods. These findings show that generating and optimizing skills in isolation is insufficient for sustained and efficient frontier tracking. Reliable adaptation requires tools and skills to be jointly maintained and provisioned as unified, evolving ecosystem.

sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS FOR STEWARD
sections.content: STEWARD Tracks the moving frontier efficiently. We evaluate whether the joint management of tools and skills enables STEWARD to sustain task success and efficiently track the moving capability frontier using DeepSeek-V3.2. As shown in Fig. 6, we compare STEWARD with four automated skill-based methods across six tool-ecosystem versions under the same task model, user model, and evaluation protocol. In Fig. 6(a), STEWARD achieves the highest SR at every version, averaging 39.04% versus 36.36% for SkillOpt, showing that its advantage persists beyond initial skill construction as the ecosystem evolves. Fig. 6(b) further shows that STEWARD incurs the lowest maintenance cost from v2 onward, with the baselines consuming 1.25.5 as many skill-maintenance tokens. Thus, the higher task success is achieved without increasing skill-update expenditure, distinguishing STEWARD from methods that rely on increasingly costly skill generation or optimization. To examine whether this advantage extends beyond SR, Fig. 6(c) reports the percentage-point gain of STEWARD over the strongest baseline for each version and metric. Most notably, STEWARD improves Step-/Cost-IDR by 4.04%/3.69% and Step-/Cost-DAR by 5.28%/4.76% on average, showing that its advantage extends from current-version success to discovering improved paths and recovering from degraded ones across ecosystem changes. These dynamic gains are accompanied by average Step-/Cost-SPE improvements of 2.68%/4.21% and consistent gains in tool precision, recall, and F1, indicating more efficient execution and more effective capability provisioning. Together, these results establish that STEWARD combines stronger frontier tracking with lower maintenance overhead, motivating the following analyses of which management mechanisms produce these gains. We ablate capability provisioning on DeepSeek-V3.2 by taking initial task view construction as the baseline and adding dynamic skill search, tool search, or both. As shown in Fig. 7, skill search alone yields little improvement in SR, SPE, IDR, or Tool F1, indicating that procedural knowledge is difficult to operationalize when the corresponding tools are not dynamically exposed. Combining both modules improves every metric; relative to tool search alone, Full Provisioning raises Step-/Cost-DAR by 11.41%/9.30% percentage points and Tool F1 by 4.90% points. These results show that tool search exposes valid implementations while skill search supplies the procedural guidance needed to use them, making their joint management essential for capability provisioning. sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Benchmarks for Tool-Using Agents. As LLMs become autonomous agents, tool ecosystems mediate discovery and use of external capabilities, motivating benchmarks spanning broader tool-use lifecycle (Qu et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025b). Early benchmarks assess API selection, argument generation, multi-tool composition, and planning (Patil et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b; 2025a). Stateful successors evaluate multi-turn interaction in environments with persistent tool effects, where success requires satisfying user constraints (Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Barrès et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Complementary benchmarks study retrieval from large, heterogeneous tool repositories (Xu et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026d), while efficiency-oriented benchmarks evaluate resource constraints, planning or operational costs, and replanning under changing costs, preferences, or tool availability (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Hazra et al., 2024; Kokel et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026e). Recent work probes robustness through API-level perturbations or controlled mutations of MCP servers (Chen et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026c). Yet these capabilities remain largely evaluated in isolation, leaving the end-to-end tool-use lifecycle in evolving ecosystems underexplored. τ -Bench addresses this gap as the first benchmark unifying large-scale tool retrieval, multi-turn stateful execution, and efficiency-aware adaptation within controlled, evolving tool ecosystem. Skill Learning and Evolution for LLM Agents. Agents should convert interaction experience into reusable procedural knowledge for continual improvement. Early work distills trajectories into natural-language guidance or reusable workflows, while later methods represent skills as executable or compositional routines (Zhao et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025b; Qiao et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Recent approaches automate skill construction and refinement through trajectory consolidation, optimization, reinforcement learning, verification, and persistent accumulation (Yang et al., 2026b; Ni et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026; He & Yang, 2026; Tang et al., 2026), with complementary work organizing growing libraries through hierarchies, dependencies, graphs, and lifecycle management (Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Pu et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026; Liang 9 Preprint. et al., 2026). Yet these methods largely evolve skills over stable operational substrate and emphasize eventual task success, leaving open whether procedural knowledge can adapt quickly enough to sustain efficient execution as the capability frontier moves. STEWARD recasts skill evolution as ecosystem-level adaptation, coupling tools with procedural knowledge to preserve reusable experience and track the evolving efficiency frontier.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce τ -Bench, an executable benchmark evaluating sustained agent competence against the moving capability frontier of large, evolving tool ecosystems. The evaluated agents struggle to sustain reliable and efficient execution, while initial gains from accumulated skills do not consistently translate into better adaptation as tools change. STEWARD couples incremental skill maintenance with dynamic provision of tools and procedural guidance, improving task performance and adaptation while reducing maintenance overhead. These results support managing tools and procedural knowledge as interdependent resources, keeping accumulated experience useful as the ecosystem evolves.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used Large Language Models solely as writing and visualization assistants during the preparation of this paper, including for refining language, improving sentence structure, and designing the presentation of selected figures. Any use of LLMs in our experiments was conducted exclusively for scientific research and has been transparently described in the Experimental Settings and Reproducibility Statement. All LLM-assisted materials were carefully reviewed by the authors. We assume full responsibility for the final manuscript and all associated content, including its text, claims, analyses, and artifacts.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This study follows established ethical principles and responsible research practices. All data were obtained or synthesized from publicly accessible sources, with no proprietary, confidential, or otherwise restricted information involved. The original sources of the data are properly acknowledged and cited throughout the paper. We expect users of our benchmark to employ it responsibly and in accordance with principles of fairness, transparency, and accountability. Applications that may cause harm or produce adverse societal consequences are not permitted.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The construction of executable environments and tasks is described in 3.1 and Appx. A.1, while ecosystem evolution and reference-path search are detailed in 3.2 and Appx. A.2. Dataset statistics are reported in Appx. A.4, and the evaluation protocol and metrics are defined in 3.3. The design of STEWARD, including incremental knowledge maintenance and dynamic provisioning of tools and skills, is presented in 5. The settings for baseline comparisons and controlled ablations are reported in 4, 6, and Appx. B. The prompts used in our study are provided in Appx. D.

DETAILS OF τ -BENCH CONSTRUCTION A.1 EXECUTABLE ENVIRONMENT AND TASK CONSTRUCTION Domain-Grounded Service Modeling. Following Sun et al. (2026), we use application domains as semantic anchors for subsequent service and environment generation. Each domain specifies coherent scope of user goals and activities, thereby preventing the generated components from becoming an arbitrary collection of unrelated concepts and operations. Starting from set of seed domains, we expand the domain pool into more specialized and role-specific scenarios and group related domains according to the activities they cover. For example, the artist-booking domain may cover activities such as identifying suitable artists, checking their availability, and arranging bookings for events. Given the resulting domain group, we identify primary user role and represent the information involved in the corresponding activities as entity schemas, each of which defines type of object and its attributes. We then construct an entityrelationship graph whose nodes represent entity types and whose edges encode the semantic relationships between them. Based on coherent subsets of entities and relationships in this graph, we derive service blueprints that define the intended users, maintained information, and available functions of each service. Each function is further described by its functional purpose, required and optional parameters, and returned information. In the artist-booking example, booking coordinator serves as the primary user, while artist, client, event, and booking constitute the main entity types. The entityrelationship graph may associate each booking with client, an artist, and an event, providing the semantic basis for functions that retrieve candidate artists, check their availability, and create bookings. After validation, each function is deterministically converted into function-calling interface containing function name and natural-language description, together with JSON Schema object that specifies the names, types, descriptions, required fields, and enumeration constraints of its input parameters. The resulting interfaces form the tool-call action space Atool for each service. From Service Blueprints to Stateful Environments. The service blueprints and function interfaces specify what each service should support, but they do not yet provide an environment in which the functions can be executed and their effects can persist. We first instantiate each entity schema with concrete records and materialize the relationships between these records in mock database. The resulting records and relationships collectively define the initial external state sE 0 , after being checked against the corresponding schema and relational constraints. In the artist-booking example, the stateful database sE 0 may contain concrete artists, clients, events, and bookings, with each booking record referring to specific client, artist, and event. database alone, however, does not determine when function may be invoked or how it changes the environment sE . We then define operational policies that specify each functions preconditions, parameter semantics, execution constraints, state changes, and cross-function dependencies. Using the function interfaces as callable contracts and the operational policies as behavioral specifications, we implement the function as executable server-side code in the MCP service. Concretely, each implementation is Python function registered under the name and input schema declared by the corresponding interface. When invoked, it receives the supplied arguments, validates them against the schema, resolves the referenced records, enforces the applicable operational constraints, and performs the required read or write operations on the mock database. It then converts the execution result or encountered error into the return format declared by the interface. Each node represents function, while directed edge indicates an execution dependency between two functions. valid path sampled on this graph naturally provides an executable structure that can be transformed into multiple coordinated tool-call task. To obtain diverse candidate structures, we sample paths from the graph by first drawing starting node from weighted probability distribution over eligible functions. Because many user tasks follow readbefore-write pattern, first locating or inspecting target entities and then modifying them, we assign higher starting probabilities to query-type functions that retrieve information without changing sE . 17 Preprint. This preference is probabilistic rather than hard constraint, allowing state-changing functions to remain possible starting points when their preconditions are already satisfied. The shared function provides an explicit semantic connection between the two sequences and serves as an anchor for organizing them under unified task objective. Second, we select an intermediate subpath and repeat it one or more times to model tasks that require iterating the same group of operations. DETAILS OF SKILL-BASED BASELINES AutoSkill (Yang et al., 2026b) extracts reusable skills from user inputs to support continual improvement without updating model parameters. It maintains skill library by adding distinct capabilities and merging refinements into existing skills, while filtering unsuitable or redundant candidates. For subsequent requests, relevant skills are retrieved and injected into the agents context to guide its responses. Trace2Skill (Ni et al., 2026) distills experience from successful and failed execution trajectories into reusable skill directory. Separate analysts process trajectories in parallel to propose skill patches, which are hierarchically consolidated to resolve conflicts and retain generalizable procedures. The resulting skill guides subsequent execution without parameter updates or retrieval of individual trajectory memories. EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026) discovers and refines reusable skills through iterative failure analysis. proposer diagnoses unsuccessful executions and suggests new or revised skills, which skill-builder turns into structured skill folders containing procedural instructions and optional supporting resources. Candidate agent programs are evaluated on held-out validation data, and the highest-scoring programs are retained for further evolution while the underlying model remains frozen. SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026a) optimizes natural-language skill document while keeping the target model fixed. separate optimizer model converts scored execution trajectories into textual edits under limited edit budget, and each update is accepted only if it improves held-out validation performance. Rejected edits provide feedback for future proposals, while consolidation across epochs preserves longer-term lessons. For all baselines, we directly adapt their official implementations to τ -Bench without revising any modules and use DeepSeek-V3.2 as the common backbone.

Planning skills describe task-level workflows, while atomic skills encode reusable operations with explicit tool dependencies. Tool skills provide invocation guidance for individual tools. Each atomic skill stores name, description, reusable usage guidance, and its required tools. The skill graph links planning skills to associated atomic skills and atomic skills to the tool skills corresponding to their dependencies. At = 1, we initialize the library following (Wang et al., 2026). Planning and atomic skills are extracted from training trajectories that pass environment-state evaluation. Planning extraction groups tool calls by their underlying subgoals, removing exploration, debugging, and failed attempts while preserving execution order. Atomic extraction focuses on one specified tool at time, replacing task-specific values with reusable parameters and retaining relevant coordination with other tools. Tool-skill summarization additionally combines tool schemas with repeated tool-call failure evidence to identify invocation constraints and recovery procedures. At the start of each episode, STEWARD retrieves the top five planning skills using the initial user request and asks an LLM to rewrite them into task-specific provisional plan ˆp. This produces structured list of actionable steps without modifying the stored planning skills. For each step, the manager retrieves up to five atomic skills subject to similarity threshold. Candidates linked to the retrieved planning skills receive priority, followed by deduplication and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to balance relevance and diversity. An LLM then selects at most 8 atomic skills based on the request and provisional plan. Their linked tool skills are attached to provide detailed invocation guidance, together forming the initial procedural context k(v) 0 . To complement skill-based retrieval, the manager directly retrieves the top three tools for each plan step. The union of these tools and the selected skills declared dependencies is intersected with the current tool catalog to obtain the initial visible set (cid:98)A(v) 0 . The visible tools and procedural context constitute the initial task-specific view b(v) 0 . The skill context is supplied as system message at each turn without appending repeated copies to the dialogue history. It instructs the task agent to apply skills only when relevant and to rely on the actual session tool list when deciding which tools can be called. Prompts for this process are shown in Appx. D.3. On-Demand Capability Provisioning. During execution, the task agent can call retrieve _tools with focused capability query to retrieve up to five additional tools when its current tool set is insufficient. For gaps requiring further investigation, it can call explore_capabilities to delegate focused search to the manager, with at most three delegations per episode. Each request specifies the task goal and missing capability, optionally including previously failed attempts. The manager also receives recent user messages and tool errors, the provisional plan, and the names of already visible tools and injected skills. It searches the active skill library and full tool catalog, using skill bodies and graph links to recover relevant procedural guidance. During this investigation, the manager cannot execute service tools or communicate with the user, and it must inspect each candidate tools schema before recommending it. If referenced tool no longer exists, it searches for semantically equivalent replacement and explicitly reports the substitution. Among equivalent options, the prompt favors lower cost or latency. The investigation operates within an action budget and ends as soon as the delegated request can be answered. The manager returns compact report specifying recommended tools and an actionable workflow, together with relevant pitfalls and rejected alternatives. At most 8 tools are returned per investigation, and programmatic check admits only tools present in the current catalog into the task agents visible set. When summarization would lose parameter-level or ordering details, the manager can additionally provide the full text of at most two skills. Skill-body delivery is limited to 4,000 characters cumulatively per episode, and each new added-skills block replaces the previous block. Providing skill does not automatically expose its referenced tools, which must be inspected and admitted separately. These outputs jointly update the available tools (cid:98)A(v) as execution reveals new capability requirements. Please refer to Appx.
